sentences.text: Specimens of M. dacus measure between 2.16 and 2.82 meters long and weigh up to 660 to 972 kg, though other estimates suggest a weight of 1.1 tons or one ton with a length of 6 meters.
Fourteen fossil eggs have been discovered and attributed to Magyarosaurus.

Remains of at least ten individuals were recovered starting in 1895 from the Hunedoara region in what was then Hungary but is now western Romania. The species was initially named Titanosaurus dacus by Baron Nopcsa in 1915 and later renamed Magyarosaurus dacus by Friedrich von Huene in 1932.
No skull remains are known for Magyarosaurus.
Histological studies show that Magyarosaurus had a very reduced growth rate but maintained a high metabolic rate.

A 2005 study found Magyarosaurus to be a close relative of Rapetosaurus within the family Saltasauridae and the sauropod clade Titanosauria. Its parent group is Eutitanosauria, and it belongs to the class Saurischia.

Friedrich von Huene reassigned the taxon to the new genus Magyarosaurus in 1932 and named two additional species, M. hungaricus and M. transsylvanicus. Other species, M. hungaricus and M. transsylvanicus, were synonymized with M. dacus by Le Loeuff in 1993 and Upchurch et al. in 2004.
Magyarosaurus dacus is known from the early Maastrichtian of the Sânpetru Formation in the Hațeg Basin, Romania. It lived from 72.2 to 66 million years ago during the Maastrichtian.

The Hațeg Basin environment changed from subhumid with seasonal precipitation in the early Maastrichtian to an extensive wetland in the later age of the formation. In the early Maastrichtian, the Hațeg Basin was subhumid with seasonal rainfall. During the late age of the formation, the region transformed into an extensive wetland.

While some researchers initially suggested Magyarosaurus fossils represented juveniles, a 2010 study of bone growth patterns supported the hypothesis that they were adults. Later researchers doubted the island dwarfism hypothesis, suggesting instead that the known Magyarosaurus fossils represented juveniles. It is debated whether M. hungaricus, which is larger and less frequent, represents a distinct taxon.
